data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The fetch budget must be denominated solely in requests, because request count is the only deterministic, replayable unit that is immune to content-length variability and caching effects. Bytes are eliminated as a weaker rival because response sizes can vary across replays due to compression, server state, or dynamic content, breaking auditability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent can make requests of vastly different sizes, a request budget may allow excessive data transfer, but this can be mitigated by a separate data cap if needed; however, for replayability, requests are deterministic.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the agent uses caching, cache hits must not count as requests, but the cache state must be part of the agent's deterministic state hash to ensure replay consistency.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the agent makes parallel requests, atomicity of the counter must be ensured via a lock or atomic operations.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The agent is configured with a maximum request count N. Each fetch attempt (including retries for transient errors) decrements a counter. Before any fetch, the agent checks if the counter would drop below zero; if so, it terminates with a typed terminal state 'request_budget_exhausted', recording the total requests made, the budget limit, and the reason. The terminal state is hashed into the agent's state log for audit. Retries are counted to prevent infinite loops, and a separate retry allowance can be configured to avoid flaky networks causing premature exhaustion, but the retry count is always recorded.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
